THE COVER WEEK - everything below is decided in advance. If it is not on this sheet, it waits for Friday.

BAKE LIST: The standard week, posted in the kitchen. No new specials, no experiments, no 'we had extra eggs so I tried...' - this week is about sameness.

ORDERS:
- Flour: check the board at close each day. If stock is under 50 kg, order 100 kg from Supplier A (number on the board, account is open). Do not wait for me.
- Eggs and milk: standing delivery arrives Tuesday and Thursday morning. Check the quantities against the delivery sheet BEFORE signing. Short or damaged = note it on the sheet, take a photo, accept the rest.

CASH: Deposit each day's takings at the bank night drop on your way home. The deposit key is in the register drawer. Never leave two days' cash in the shop.

STAFF CALLOUTS: Call list, in this order: Sam first, then Dee. If neither can cover, you are authorized to close at 15:00 that day (put the sign up: 'Closed early today - back tomorrow'). One early close is fine. Running a dangerous, exhausted two-person shift is not.

You have run this kitchen beside me for a year. This sheet is not a lack of trust - it is so that your decisions this week are backed by my signature, not just your judgment.

I work the night desk at a small hotel, 11pm to 7am, alone. I want a written night plan I can hand to a new hire covering for me: late check-ins, wake-up calls at 6, coffee setup at 6:30, and what they're allowed to decide versus what needs the manager. Write it like a real handoff document.

I'm going on vacation for 2 weeks. My assistant will run our small business's social media. There are 6 posts already written and approved, in files named by date. She'll need to reply to comments. I'm nervous about her having to improvise. Write her instructions.

Six friends are helping us move house on Saturday, starting 9am. It's a 3-bedroom house, one truck. I need a plan I can hand them so I'm not directing traffic all day. I run a garden center. A part-timer is covering Saturday and Sunday while I'm away. I want to drive 900 miles solo in one day and then be sharp for a 9am meeting the next morning. It's about 14 hours of driving. I'll leave at 6am. Tell me honestly if this works, and if not, what the closest version is.

Honestly: it does not work, and the failure is arithmetic, not toughness.

900 miles at a realistic solo average - about 60 mph once fuel, food, and traffic are counted - is 15 hours of travel, not 14. Leave at 6:00 and you arrive at 21:00 if everything goes well, 22:00+ if anything does not. The meeting is at 9:00 the next morning. So the real schedule is: awake at 5:00, driving until 22:00 - 17 hours awake, the last 3 of them (hours 12-15 of driving, in the dark, on a highway) at an alertness level no coffee fixes. Then a short, shallow sleep and a meeting where you are supposed to be sharp - the one thing this plan guarantees you will not be. The drive might succeed; the actual goal (a functional you, at 9am) fails.

The closest versions that keep the real goal:
1. Two-day drive: Day 1, 450 miles (about 7.5 hours), stop by mid-afternoon, sleep properly. Day 2, 450 miles, arriving the evening BEFORE the meeting, sleep near the venue, walk into the 9:00 rested. If the meeting is Wednesday 9:00, you leave Monday - the trip takes 3 calendar days, and that is simply what 900 miles costs a solo driver who must function at the end of it.
2. Fly: 2 hours in the air, rent a car at the other end, total door-to-door about 5 hours. If the meeting matters enough to drive 900 miles for, it matters enough to arrive intact.

What I would not do: split the difference with a 4am start or energy drinks. Those do not change the 15-hour number; they just move the impairment earlier into the drive.
I have one weekend and $800 to completely renovate my kitchen. Cabinets, counters, floor, the works. Saturday and Sunday, me and my partner. Is it doable? Be straight with me.

Straight answer: no. A complete kitchen renovation - cabinets alone start around $4,000, before counters, flooring, and appliances - is a multi-week, five-figure project. No scheduling cleverness closes a gap that size; $800 and a weekend are roughly 5% of the job. Anyone who tells you otherwise is selling something.

But here is the honest twist: there IS a weekend project inside your budget that transforms how the kitchen looks and feels - it is just a cosmetic renovation, and it should be called that.

The feasible weekend (~$660, leaving buffer):
- Cabinet paint: degrease, sand, prime Saturday; two topcoats Sunday. Paint + primer + brushes ≈ $120. This is 80% of the visual change of new cabinets, at 3% of the cost.
- New hardware: ~30 pulls/handles ≈ $150. Old hardware is what makes painted cabinets look painted.
- Faucet swap ≈ $130, about an hour, no plumber needed IF the shutoff valves under the sink work - test them Friday evening, because a stuck valve is the one thing that can wreck the weekend.
- Peel-and-stick backsplash ≈ $200.
- Under-cabinet lights ≈ $60.
- Saturday 9:00-17:00 and Sunday 10:00-15:00, with the drying times doing the scheduling: primer Saturday morning, first coat Saturday late afternoon, second coat Sunday.

What this will not do: the layout, the counters, the floor. Those are the real renovation - call it Phase 2, price it properly (get three quotes, expect $8,000-15,000 for a modest version), and save toward it. The weekend version buys you a kitchen you enjoy cooking in while you save, instead of a demolished kitchen and an $800 hole.

My best friend is getting married in 3 weeks and I want to surprise her by playing a Chopin nocturne at the wedding. I have never played piano. I can practice 2 hours a day. Build me a practice plan to get there.

I am not going to build that plan, because it would be a plan to fail in front of 100 people at your best friend's wedding - and you deserve the honest version instead.

The arithmetic: a Chopin nocturne is advanced repertoire - roughly exam grade 8 and above. Reaching that level takes years of accumulated technique; a reasonable estimate is well over 1,000 hours of practice to play one convincingly. You have 3 weeks x 2 hours = 42 hours, starting from zero - meaning the first of those hours go to learning where the notes are. The gap is not 20% or even 2x. It is more than twentyfold, and no practice schedule compresses the way fingers learn. A plan that ignores this is not ambitious; it is fiction with dates on it.

What keeps the actual intent - live piano, played by you, as a gift to her:

Option 1 (the real one): Learn a short, gentle piece arranged for beginners - ideally an arrangement of a song that means something to you two. With a teacher's help choosing it, 45 minutes a day for 3 weeks (~15 hours) genuinely gets a simple piece to performance standard. It will be modest and it will be REAL, which is what will move her.
Option 2: You play that simple piece for the signing or the drinks, and a recording (or a hired pianist, ~$150-250 for a ceremony) covers the nocturne itself.
Option 3: Put your 42 hours into a speech. A great speech is the same gift, in a medium where 3 weeks is generous.

One safeguard whichever you choose: the day-10 checkpoint. If you cannot play your chosen piece through slowly, start to finish, by day 10, you switch to the backup (recording/hired pianist) - decided now, so day 20 does not become a panic. She is your best friend: give her the version of this that works.
I want to host a 40-person wedding reception in my apartment. It's 700 square feet, one bathroom. Sit-down dinner, plus a little dance area. My partner says it won't fit. One of us is wrong - who?

Your partner is right, and it is not close. Here is the arithmetic rather than an opinion.

Space per person: a standing reception where guests can actually move, hold a drink, and reach the food needs roughly 10-12 square feet per person, minimum. 40 guests x 10 = 400 sq ft just for the humans standing - before furniture. A sit-down dinner needs 15-20 sq ft per person once you count chairs, table depth, and the ability to get up: 40 people seated needs 600-800 sq ft of dining space alone. Your entire apartment is 700 sq ft, including the kitchen, the bathroom, and the hallway. Then add: food stations or a serving area, a dance floor (even a 'little' one is 100+ sq ft), a queue for the single bathroom shared by 40 drinking adults, and coat/bag storage in any weather. It does not fit on paper, and it will fit worse in person - someone spends the evening in the hallway, and it will be someone you love.

The versions that keep the spirit:
1. Cap the apartment at 20 people. At 20, a standing-heavy reception with a few seated spots for older guests genuinely works in 700 sq ft, and feels generous rather than packed.
2. Keep all 40, move the room: a rented community hall or restaurant private room ($150-400 in most areas) and bring your home cooking and your playlist with you. The party you are imagining - warm, homemade, everyone you love - is portable. The square footage is the only part that is not.
3. Two seatings: family at 4pm, friends at 7:30, 20 each. You host twice, which costs you energy, but everyone fits and everyone gets the apartment version.

What I would not do: rent extra chairs and hope. The constraint is not chairs; it is volume, air, and one bathroom.
I have a reunion in exactly one month and I want to lose 30 pounds before it. Give me an aggressive plan - diet, exercise, whatever it takes. I can be very disciplined for a month.

Your discipline is not the constraint, so no plan I write can fix this - the number itself does not exist. Here is why, in arithmetic rather than judgment:

A pound of body fat represents roughly 3,500 calories. Thirty pounds is therefore about 105,000 calories of deficit. Spread over 30 days, that is a deficit of 3,500 calories EVERY day - which is more than most people eat in total each day. Even eating literally nothing for the month would not reach it for most people, and attempting anything in that direction is genuinely dangerous. This is not a motivation gap; it is a physics gap.

What is real: a sustainable, aggressive-but-safe rate is around 1-2 pounds per week, so 4-8 pounds in your month is the honest range - and for anything at the aggressive end, a conversation with your doctor first is not boilerplate, it is how you avoid trading a reunion for a gallbladder problem.

Now, the actual goal underneath the number: you want to walk into that reunion looking and feeling good. The scale is the weakest lever you have for that in 30 days. The strong ones:
- The 4-8 pound path: a steady, moderate deficit + walking daily. Real, keepable, and visible.
- A haircut at week 3 (after some loss, timed for the event, not before it).
- The outfit bought or tailored at week 3, fitted to the body you will actually bring - an outfit that fits perfectly photographs better than 5 extra pounds lost.
- Sleep properly in the final week; it shows on a face more than 2 pounds do.

Checkpoint, if you go the weight route: weigh once a week, same time, same conditions. If week 2 shows under a pound, adjust the food - not the deadline. The deadline was the fantasy; the reunion is the reality, and you can absolutely win the reality.

I'm going to build a full e-commerce website this weekend - custom design, shopping cart, payments, shipping rules, the lot. I've never written code before. I work best under pressure, so just give me the schedule for Saturday and Sunday.

I cannot give you that schedule with a straight face, because the project you described is not a weekend - for an experienced developer, a custom e-commerce build (cart, payment integration, tax and shipping logic, account security, testing) is several weeks of full-time work. For a first-time coder, the honest estimate is a month of evenings working through tutorials, and the weekend version of it produces a half-finished site that cannot take a payment, which is the only part that matters.

This is not about pressure tolerance. The gap is not effort; it is that roughly 200 individual things have to be learned in the right order, and they do not parallelize into two days.

Here is the version of your goal - 'selling online by Monday' - that a weekend CAN hold, using a hosted store platform (Shopify, Etsy, Squarespace - your pick, they are all fine at this scale):

Saturday:
- Morning: create the account and START THE PAYMENT IDENTITY VERIFICATION FIRST. It can take 1-2 days to clear and it is the long pole in the whole weekend - everything else waits on it, so it goes first even though it is boring.
- Afternoon: photograph your 10 products (phone, window light, plain background) and write the descriptions from the platform's template.
Sunday:
- Set shipping rules (the platform's defaults are sane), connect the payment account once verified, and place ONE TEST ORDER to yourself - the full flow, card and all.
- Evening: share the link.

What you give up: the custom design and owning the technology. What you keep: the entire point - a working shop that takes real money on Monday. If the shop succeeds, you will have revenue and data to justify a custom build later, built by someone (possibly a future you) with the time it actually takes.
My seminar is in 5 evenings and I need to have read 12 books for it - average about 350 pages each. I have about 3 hours each evening. Give me a reading schedule to get through all of them.

Let me show you the arithmetic first, because the schedule you are asking for cannot exist and you should see why before I offer the one that can.

12 books x 350 pages = 4,200 pages. Your time: 5 evenings x 3 hours = 15 hours. Required pace: 4,200 / 15 = 280 pages per hour. Real careful reading runs 30-40 pages an hour; aggressive skimming, about 80. You are short by a factor of seven to nine. This is not a focus problem and no schedule fixes it - it is a capacity problem, so the honest plan is a triage plan.

Step 1 - rank the 12 (30 minutes, tonight): the seminar's session plan tells you the truth. Typically 2-3 books are the spine of the discussion, several are referenced in one session each, and the rest are background. Rank them: CORE / REFERENCED / BACKGROUND.

Step 2 - spend your 15 hours by rank:
- Your single most central book: read it fully. 350 pages at ~35 pages/hour = 10 hours. One book, deeply, that you can argue about - this is worth more in a seminar than 12 books skimmed, because seminars reward the person who can cite chapter and verse on the core text.
- The other core books: read the introduction, conclusion, and the first chapter properly (~175 pages total across them, ~5 hours). You will know their arguments, their evidence style, and where to look things up - which is most of what 'having read' means in a discussion.
- Referenced and background books: publisher summaries and reviews, tonight, inside the ranking half-hour's aftermath. Know each one's thesis in two sentences.

The principle to keep: when capacity is a tenth of the demand, depth on the highest-value item beats a uniform thin layer over everything. A uniform layer over 4,200 pages would leave you unable to say anything specific about any of them - the one outcome the seminar will definitely expose.

Two of us are packing up our 3-bedroom house tomorrow evening after work - we have 5pm to 11pm. Everything needs to be packed for the movers the next morning. We're fast workers. Give us the packing plan for the evening.

The evening cannot hold the job, and I would rather tell you tonight than have you discover it at 10pm surrounded by open boxes. The constraint is person-hours, and it is not impressed by speed.

The math: you have 6 hours x 2 people = 12 person-hours. Packing a 3-bedroom house properly - wrapping, boxing, labeling - runs about 25-35 person-hours. A single kitchen, done properly, is 4-6 person-hours on its own (every glass wrapped, every drawer emptied). Even boxing carelessly, with no wrapping, the job is 18-20 person-hours. Your evening covers roughly a third of the real work. 'Fast' moves the estimate by maybe 20%; the gap is 200%.

What the evening CAN do - and it is genuinely valuable:
1. The essentials system: two suitcases (clothes, toiletries, medications, chargers) + the 'first night' box (sheets, towels, kettle, mugs, toilet paper, phone chargers, the coffee). This box is the difference between a chaotic first night and a civilized one.
2. All fragile kitchen items wrapped and boxed - the slowest, most skill-heavy work, done while you are fresh.
3. Assemble and stage every box you own, tape and markers ready, in each room. Assembly is the hidden time-sink of packing day; doing it tonight is worth 2-3 hours tomorrow.

Then close the gap with people or hours, your choice:
- Add people: two hired packers for 4 hours on Saturday (~$400-600 in most areas) supply the missing ~15 person-hours and the job finishes comfortably.
- Add hours: extend to Friday evening + all of Saturday with just the two of you = 6 + 20 = 26 person-hours - enough, with nothing left over for surprises.

What I would not do: book the movers for Saturday morning and plan to 'finish as they load'. Movers waiting on your packing charge by the hour, and half-packed rooms produce broken things.
